title: $250,000 Mortgage Payment by Rate & Term (2026)
metaDescription: A $250,000 mortgage costs $1,580.17/mo at 6.5% over 30 years ($2,177.77 on 15). See payments at 5–7.5%, total interest, and the income needed.

hero.lede: Principal-and-interest payments on a $250,000 home loan across 5.0%–7.5% rates and 15/30-year terms, plus total interest, a first-year amortization schedule, and the income the 28% rule implies.

shortAnswer.heading: What does a $250,000 mortgage cost per month?
shortAnswer.html: A $250,000 mortgage costs about $1,580.17 a month in principal and interest at 6.5% on a 30-year fixed term, or $2,177.77 on a 15-year. Depending on your rate (5.0%–7.5%), the 30-year payment runs $1,342.05–$1,748.04. Total 30-year interest at 6.5%: $318,861.

sections.title: $250,000 mortgage payment by rate and term.
sections.note: Principal and interest only — add property taxes, homeowners insurance, and PMI (if under 20% down) for the full monthly cost.

sections.title: What $250,000 of mortgage debt really costs.
paragraphs: At today's representative 6.5% rate, $250,000 of mortgage debt runs $1,580.17 a month on a 30-year term, or $2,177.77 on a 15-year. Over the full term that's $318,861 of interest versus $141,999 — a $176,863 difference for the faster payoff.

A single percentage point matters enormously at this size: 6.0% versus 7.0% on a 30-year $250,000 loan is $164.38 more every month, or about $59,177 over 360 payments. That's why the payment table spans $1,342.05 (at 5.0%) to $1,748.04 (at 7.5%).

sections.title: Total interest on $250,000 over the full term.
sections.note: At 6.5% on a 30-year term you repay $568,861 in total — 2.28× the amount borrowed.

sections.title: First-year amortization: where each payment actually goes.
sections.note: In year one you pay $16,168 of interest but only $2,794 of principal — early payments are mostly interest, which is why extra principal payments early on save so much.

sections.title: PMI, income needed, and the rest of the bill.
paragraphs: If your down payment is under 20% of the purchase price, expect private mortgage insurance on top: typically 0.5–1% of the loan per year, or roughly $104–$208 a month on $250,000. With 20% down, a $250,000 loan corresponds to about a $312,500 home — and no PMI. Property taxes and homeowners insurance also come on top of every figure here.

Lenders often screen affordability with the 28% rule: housing below 28% of gross income. Covering $1,580.17 a month of P&I under that rule takes about $67,722 a year of income. Because taxes and insurance stack on top, real qualifying incomes run higher.

sections.title: Nearby loan amounts at 6.5%.
sections.note: Income column applies the 28% front-end rule to the 30-year P&I payment only; taxes and insurance push the real requirement higher.

faq.q: What is the monthly payment on a $250,000 mortgage?
faq.a: At 6.5% on a 30-year fixed, a $250,000 mortgage costs $1,580.17 a month in principal and interest. Across rates from 5.0% to 7.5%, the 30-year payment ranges from $1,342.05 to $1,748.04. Property taxes, insurance, and PMI come on top.

faq.q: How much income do I need for a $250,000 mortgage?
faq.a: Using the 28% front-end rule on the $1,580.17 payment (6.5%, 30-year), you'd want roughly $67,722 of gross annual income for the principal and interest alone. Since lenders count taxes, insurance, PMI, and your other debts too, a comfortable qualifying income is typically higher.

faq.q: How much interest will I pay on a $250,000 mortgage?
faq.a: At 6.5%, total interest comes to $318,861 over a 30-year term versus $141,999 over 15 years — the shorter term saves $176,863. In the first year alone the 30-year loan accrues $16,168 of interest against just $2,794 of principal reduction.

faq.q: Is a 15-year or 30-year term better for a $250,000 loan?
faq.a: The 30-year payment ($1,580.17 at 6.5%) is $597.60 cheaper per month than the 15-year ($2,177.77), but costs $176,863 more in lifetime interest. Choose 15 years if the payment fits comfortably; otherwise take the 30-year and make extra principal payments when you can.

faq.q: Does the $250,000 payment include taxes and insurance?
faq.a: No — every figure on this page is principal and interest only. Budget extra for property tax and homeowners insurance (often several hundred dollars monthly, varying by state), plus PMI of roughly $104–$208/month if your down payment is under 20%. With 20% down, $250,000 of financing corresponds to about a $312,500 purchase price.

methodology: Payments use the standard amortization formula M = P·r(1+r)ⁿ / ((1+r)ⁿ − 1) with monthly compounding, on a $250,000 principal. Rates shown (5.0%–7.5%) are illustrative steps, not quotes — your rate depends on credit, points, and the market.
The amortization table applies 6.5%/30-year, computing interest on the running balance each month and rounding to cents, the way a servicer statement does.
All figures are principal and interest only. Property tax, homeowners insurance, HOA dues, and PMI are excluded except where explicitly estimated (PMI shown at 0.5–1% of the loan per year).
Income-needed figures apply the 28% front-end ratio to P&I only. Educational estimates — not lending, tax, or financial advice.
